items.definition: A physical change alters the form of a substance (e.g., its phase) without altering its chemical identity and can be undone, while a chemical change (such as combustion) transforms a substance into something new and generally cannot be reversed.
items.core_idea: The defining test between the two types of change is reversibility: melting and refreezing water returns it to its original state, but burning or cooking a substance permanently changes it.
key_points: Chemical properties describe how a substance reacts with other substances (e.g., combustion is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen).
Physical properties describe changes that don't alter chemical identity.
Reversibility is the practical dividing line: physical (state) changes reverse, chemical reactions generally don't.
Most real-world mixtures undergo some combination of both physical and chemical changes as temperature changes, and under some conditions a solid can convert straight to a gas.
relationships: Underpins why distillation/refining (physical) differ fundamentally from combustion (chemical) as industrial processes.
trading_implications: Because combustion is one-way, burnt/consumed fuel can't be recovered, which is part of why fuel is treated as a consumable commodity rather than a reusable asset.
common_misunderstandings: Not all temperature-driven transformations are simple phase changes; some are irreversible chemical reactions even though both are triggered by heating.
related_topics: Phase (State of Matter) and Its Trading Relevance

items.topic: Phase (State of Matter) and Its Trading Relevance
items.definition: Phase is whether a substance is solid, liquid, or gas; it determines how a fuel must be transported and what kind of equipment or engine is needed to use it.
items.core_idea: Because phase governs transport and end-use equipment requirements, controlling phase changes deliberately (distillation, air conditioning) is central to energy processes, while uncontrolled phase changes (like unwanted condensation) can damage equipment.
key_points: Solids and liquids stay contained in a vessel; gas dissipates immediately unless actively contained.
Controlled state changes (distillation, refrigeration/AC) are deliberate and useful.
Uncontrolled state changes (e.g., condensation in a pipeline) can be destructive.
The physical phase of a fuel dictates the transport method and the combustion/engine technology required to use it.
relationships: Connects to pipeline design considerations and to distillation/refrigeration as controlled-phase-change industries.
trading_implications: A fuel's phase is a structural constraint on its logistics and market infrastructure, not just a technical detail — it shapes which transport and end-use assets a trader must account for.
related_topics: States of Matter: Solid, Liquid, Gas

items.topic: Melting Point and Boiling Point as Separation Tools
items.definition: Every substance has its own distinct melting point (solid/liquid transition) and boiling point (liquid/gas transition), and because these thresholds differ substance to substance, a mixture can be separated by carefully controlling temperature.
items.core_idea: Slowly heating a mixture causes its components to melt or vaporize off one at a time in order of their unique transition temperatures, which is the physical basis for separating raw materials into purified products.
key_points: Boiling point governs liquid/gas transitions; melting point governs solid/liquid transitions.
Because each substance's transition points are unique, controlled heating separates components sequentially.
This principle underlies purification tasks like extracting gasoline from crude oil or separating ethanol from water.
relationships: Directly enables distillation as a separation method.
trading_implications: Separation via temperature control (rather than chemical reaction) explains why refining is energy-intensive: the heating/cooling needed to hit precise transition points consumes significant energy, a cost embedded in refined product economics.

items.definition: Distillation is a purely physical separation process where a liquid mixture is heated until it boils, and the resulting vapor is captured and cooled back into liquid form, isolating components by their differing boiling points.
items.core_idea: Distillation separates and identifies liquid mixtures (including unknown hydrocarbon blends) using heat alone, with no chemical reaction involved, and is a large energy consumer due to the heating and cooling required.
key_points: Process: heat mixture to boiling, capture the vapor, cool it back to liquid.
It is a physical process, not a chemical one — no new substances are created.
It is commonly used to separate liquids and to identify unknown hydrocarbon liquids.
Like refrigeration, it requires a tremendous amount of energy because of the heating and cooling involved.
relationships: Is the practical application of unique boiling/melting points; conceptually parallel to refrigeration in its heavy energy use.
trading_implications: The energy intensity of distillation is a real cost driver embedded in refined product economics and should be considered when modeling refining margins.
common_misunderstandings: Distillation is sometimes conflated with chemical refining steps, but the author is explicit that it does not rely on chemical reactions.
related_topics: Melting Point and Boiling Point as Separation Tools

items.definition: Compressing a gas heats it up (and it radiates that heat into its surroundings), while allowing a gas to expand cools it down (and it absorbs heat); liquefying a gas by compression requires substantial cooling, and without continued cooling the liquid will re-expand into gas.
items.core_idea: This heat/cool behavior under compression and expansion is the physical mechanism underlying refrigeration and air conditioning systems.
key_points: Compression raises gas temperature; the gas radiates that heat outward.
Expansion lowers gas temperature; the gas absorbs heat from its surroundings.
Turning gas into liquid via compression requires substantial cooling to counteract the heat generated.
A liquefied gas kept from staying cool will begin expanding back into gas.
relationships: Directly explains how refrigeration/AC systems work and is also the physical property causing bubble/condensation issues in pipelines.
trading_implications: This same compress/cool cycle underlies LNG production economics and refrigeration-based cooling infrastructure relevant to gas storage and transport assets.
related_topics: States of Matter: Solid, Liquid, Gas

_validation.judge_reason: Source directly states compression heats gas which radiates into environment, expansion cools gas which absorbs heat, liquefying requires substantial cooling, and unkept-cool liquid re-expands.

items.definition: Because pipeline temperatures aren't constant, unwanted phase changes can occur in transit: in gas pipelines, liquids can condense out and are extremely difficult to remove, while in oil pipelines, gas bubbles can form and damage the pipe.
items.core_idea: Pipeline engineers must design systems to handle both gas and liquid phases simultaneously because temperature variation along a pipeline can cause the transported fuel to partially change phase, creating operational hazards.
key_points: Gas pipelines: condensed liquids are hard to remove once they form.
Oil pipelines: bubble formation can damage the pipe.
Root cause is non-constant temperature along the pipeline route.
Pipeline design must accommodate both gas and liquid phases of the transported substance.
relationships: A direct consequence of the phase-transition properties described for gases and liquids.
trading_implications: Uncontrolled condensation/bubble formation represents an operational risk to transport infrastructure that can affect delivery reliability and asset integrity.
related_topics: Phase (State of Matter) and Its Trading Relevance
